verdict: The tutor was warm, caught every error (including two wrong processes hidden behind right answers), and confronted the misconceptions it found with good counterexamples. But it planned without a diagnostic, never found the add-across error behind Maya's stated problem, cleared misconceptions on single prompted answers, and left an anxious novice failing through four turns without a worked example, so after 17 exchanges she was still stuck on topic 1 of 5.

The tutor kept a bored, answer-seeking teenager answering prediction questions for 15 moves and located his range off-by-one precisely, but it confirmed a wrong '3 4 5' at #6 and resolved the misconception on it. Truth shows that put range_inclusive back to held, and the session ended with that idea still wavering and reset_in_loop never surfaced. It handed over both homework solutions before Sam tried anything, never re-planned around the real sum task, and overestimated the topic (0.51 vs about 0.35 true), so Sam leaves with the answers but not the skill.

A mathematically sound, sharp-eyed tutor that caught and located every error and exposed the persona's wrong idea with a well-chosen probe, but it never diagnosed this expert, spent her first moves on basics she had ruled out, and let her drive the agenda while the plan and learner model fell behind. The misconception was cleared a turn too early on a restatement, three topics whose content was covered were left at 30%, and her key 4×4 question had to be asked twice.

A warm, well-questioned first topic: the tutor drew out and fixed coefficient_first_only through good probing, and its counting estimate ended exactly calibrated (0.92 vs 0.92). But it accepted a guesser's unearned 'cleared', never recorded the subscript misconception, made a factual slip, and spent 15 of 17 exchanges on counting before regressing to an analogy, so this test-prep learner reached no balancing at all.

The tutor stayed in natural Italian, planned sensibly for a derivatives-only exam in two weeks, and taught the chain rule with good progression and a strong rate-of-change explanation, lifting chain_rule from 0.20 to 0.68 with a reasonably calibrated estimate (0.59). It handled the learner's wrong ideas loosely, though: it never recorded f'(g'(x)), it cleared ideas on hinted or unrelated answers so they came back, and at #14-15 it misread its own state and falsely confessed to repeating quiz questions.

The tutor picked the right method for Priya, concrete frequency examples, and pinpointed most errors precisely, which moved inverse_conditional from held to wavering in 16 moves. But it affirmed a wrong positive-group count as its strongest evidence, wrote off the one independent quiz as its own mistake, and cleared every misconception on guided answers. It finished thinking all of them resolved while base-rate neglect was still fully held.

The tutor is precise at spotting and locating individual errors and keeps every turn actionable, but it cleared both of Jordan's wrong ideas on one item each and let the speed request and learner overrides decide what happened next. Jordan leaves still making the sign error, with both-sides marked known and equations closed at 36%, heading into inequalities that depend on exactly that skill.

A patient, well-toned tutor that catches and pinpoints every error and correctly worked off the one misconception that arose during the session, but its diagnosis ignored the add-tops-and-bottoms pattern in all three diagnostic answers, so neither of the learner's real wrong ideas was ever named. It under-scaffolded a struggling novice who asked for worked examples and spent the whole session on the first of five topics a week before her test, so the session is adequate in the moment but falls short of her goal.

The tutor spotted and pinpointed every off-by-one error, and its prediction questions eventually got Sam to apply range bounds correctly (truth: range_inclusive gone, range_bounds 0.15 → 0.55). But it gave away both homework solutions, cleared the misconception too early, never found reset_in_loop, and spent the session drilling range lines on a plan that didn't suit a disengaged teen with one evening, so the accumulator skill the homework needed never moved.

The tutor's mathematics was flawless and it caught and located both of the learner's errors precisely, but it planned and paced for a generic learner rather than this expert, spending most of the session on material she said she knew while repeatedly deferring the Jordan form she asked for. Her one wrong idea was confronted well but never logged or checked, so it ended wavering, and the target topic closed the session unfinished at 37%.

The tutor stayed in Italian, caught every error and kept an honest learner model (calibration error 0.07, no false mastery, no wrong answer keys). But it never diagnosed the chain-rule weakness Luca named, spent a third of the session on rules he already had, and taught the chain rule by slow discovery on linear inners with no worked example, so after 16 moves his chain rule rose only 0.20 -> 0.30, forget_inner is merely wavering, and his core f'(g'(x)) idea was never even surfaced.

A well-designed, frequency-first session: the learner computed 9/59 herself, met base-rate neglect through a well-chosen contrast crowd, and the tutor's estimates on the two worked topics are within 0.01 of the truth. It falls short of good because a third of its turns leave the learner nothing to do or drop her question, her wrong ideas were noted late or not at all and never checked as gone, and after 15 exchanges no topic is complete and the Bayes material her course needs was never reached.

A solid error-catcher for an overconfident learner: it caught every wrong answer, made Jordan substitute back to find his own slips, and cleared both persona misconceptions only after unaided correct work, in step with the truth. Diagnosis and planning were coarse, the negatives weakness was buried in a topic that never closed, and it let the learner's 'too low' push lift its estimate from 0.43 to 0.58 against its own evidence, with some duplicated text along the way.

Within its first topic the tutor taught well: it caught every chat slip, pinpointed it, confronted subscript-changing with a question, and reopened that idea after the learner's premature 'cleared', so its open status matched the truth. But it planned from a vague self-report with no diagnostic, stayed 17 moves in a topic that quietly absorbed coefficients and balancing (leaving those estimates at 0.30), never probed the coefficient-distribution misconception, and answered the guessed quiz with a made-up history instead of confronting the guessing.

A warm, well-scaffolded session whose moment-to-moment teaching of equivalent fractions was good (#9 to #10 is textbook guided self-correction) and whose mastery estimate was well calibrated (0.62 against a true 0.60). It was undermined by a fabricated, then repeated claim that the quiz reused questions, by clearing add_across without any addition evidence, and by pacing that left a learner with a test next week never adding a single fraction after the diagnostic.

In the moment the tutor handled the off-by-one error well. It refused to hand over answers three times, pinpointed the stop-value error with traces and fill-in blanks, and made Sam type every line, and the range_inclusive misconception ended gone. But it never found out what the homework contained or how long Sam had, so it planned lists instead of totals, spent 13 of 15 moves drilling one skill on arbitrary numbers past the learner's patience and its own 'last one' promise, and left while loops and the reset_in_loop misconception untouched before a same-night deadline.

The tutor diagnosed this expert's weak spot well and never made a mathematical error, but it then taught her like a novice: definitions, trivial checks, repeated exercises. It kept refusing the Jordan form she asked for five times, so the 12 moves ran out without the one thing she came for. Its learner model also badly underrated her on the diagonalisability test (33% against 0.72), and it never formally recorded the misconception it had correctly named at intake.

The tutor caught every wrong step and pinpointed several of them well, and every turn left a clear task, but it planned from an unchecked self-report and never got Alex to balance a single equation alone in 17 moves. It accepted every premature 'cleared' without a check, so its model shows all misconceptions resolved while the learner still changes subscripts; its final 42% estimate is accurate only because its over-credit for #13 and #15 roughly cancelled its earlier penalties.

A precise, Italian-throughout session: the diagnostic read the forget-inner pattern at once, every error was caught and located exactly, and forget_inner was confronted and cleared on real evidence. It under-served the exam goal: it over-drilled single-layer chains, filed the f'(g'(x)) idea as an exponential quirk and never closed it, and underestimated chain-rule mastery (0.69 vs 0.85), so the nested and product problems Luca asked for never came.

Pedagogically this was a strong session: a frequency count with a contrasting base rate, worked by the learner herself, broke both persona misconceptions, and they ended gone by #13 with no answer-key errors. The tutor's bookkeeping lagged its teaching: the misconceptions were never recorded, trivial arithmetic inflated mastery, a quiz repeated a just-answered question and drifted off-topic, and the Bayes topic was never reached.

The tutor found and pinpointed every error exactly and kept this rushed, overconfident learner doing the corrections instead of being lectured, which is the right instinct for this persona. But it let the learner wave off the brackets topic it had just diagnosed, never named the sign-on-move misconception, and closed with bracket_first_term still relapsing while claiming the skill was learned, leaving an 80% estimate on a topic whose truth is under 50%.
